newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's fate in balance as doctors meet Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: Russia's fate in balance as doctors meet Yeltsin.

text.p: Russia's political future was in the hands of a group of doctors on Wednesday as they prepared to weigh the consequences of performing heart surgery on President Boris Yeltsin.

The doctors, joined by the pioneering U.S. heart specialist Michael DeBakey, were due to visit Moscow's elite Central Clinical Hospital where the 65-year-old leader has been under observation since September 13.

The surgery, which Yeltsin himself said was necessary if he were to continue to lead an active political life, looks certain to go ahead, although doctors have voiced caution and media speculation has been rife about possible complications.
The liberal newspaper Sevodnya said on Wednesday that, whatever the council of doctors decided, "the operation was necessary for political considerations".
The doctors, led by chief surgeon Renat Akchurin, were scheduled to meet Yeltsin (0900 GMT) to decide whether or not to go ahead with the surgery, when and how it should be performed.
But Akchurin, a former pupil of the veteran DeBakey, on Tuesday ruled out cancellation of the bypass surgery.

Sevodnya said that if the doctors cast doubt on the operation going ahead or if it were postponed for a significant period, Russia could be plunged into more uncertainty that Yeltsin's opponents were sure to exploit.

The communist opposition have already seized on the health issue, accusing Yeltsin's camp of deceiving the electorate in the July 3 vote, which gave the president another four years in office, and suggesting that he should retire if unfit.
Akchurin gave them further ammunition in a frank television interview at the weekend in which he said Yeltsin may have had a third heart attack between the first and second rounds of voting.
At the time, Yeltsin disappeared from public view but his aides insisted that he was merely exhausted and had a cold.
Yeltsin's heart problems became clear only on September 5 when he said he had opted for surgery rather than lead a passive life which had never been his style.
"Even if an operation is not necessary on patient Yeltsin, President Yeltsin will have to be operated on," Sevodnya said. "Otherwise, he can expect to face a major scandal."
"It is not clear how he could remain president after he refuses surgical intervention on the functioning of his heart."
Nevertheless, doctors have expressed concern about possible complications ranging from pneumonia to kidney failure.

Akchurin, who would lead the team performing the surgery, hinted at the weekend that the doctors may decide to put the operation off for up to eight weeks, hoping the president will be strong enough by then to withstand the operation.
On Tuesday Yeltsin appeared to have trouble speaking in a brief heavily-edited television clip released by the Kremlin.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Tuesday Yeltsin's resignation now was out of the question and condemned the opposition call. "This is totally unacceptable," he said.
Yeltsin has already handed over some powers to Chernomyrdin and said he would put the prime minister in complete charge while he is in the operating theatre.
Under the constitution, Chernomyrdin steps in if Yeltsin becomes incapacitated but there is no mechanism for this.

The president's absence from the political scene has fuelled speculation about a power struggle between Chernomyrdin and presidential administration chief Anatoly Chubais on the one hand and security supremo Alexander Lebed on the other.
